children: Polymarket

is pursuing a new funding round at a valuation of about $21 billion, even as the prediction-market operator faces questions about fraud prevention, regulatory compliance and the reliability of its U.S. platform.

The company’s problems intensified in February when criminals used stolen debit cards to attempt at least $10 million in transactions, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the incident. At one point, Polymarket’s
payment processor rejected more than 80% of deposits as potentially fraudulent, compared with an industry norm of roughly 1%.
Chief Executive Shayne Coplan allegedly urged employees to prioritize growth despite internal warnings about the attack, according to the report. Polymarket
said it's committed to fair markets and has systems for identifying and addressing suspicious activity.
The allegations create a sharp contrast between Polymarket’s

soaring valuation and its operational maturity. Investors must weigh the company’s rapid user growth and strong brand recognition against possible regulatory penalties, customer losses and the cost of building more robust compliance systems. The controversies also present risks for Intercontinental Exchange, which reported owning 22% of Polymarket, and for other investors backing the company’s expansion.
Scrutiny grows
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating Polymarket
, while New York City officials are examining advertising by the company and its competitors. Nearly two dozen traders have accused Polymarket
of deceptive practices in lawsuits.
More than a dozen state cases also challenge whether prediction markets offered by Polymarket
, Kalshi
and Coinbase
amount to unlicensed gambling. The results could determine how widely these platforms may offer contracts tied to sports, politics and other events.

Polymarket entered the regulated U.S. market after acquiring a licensed exchange for $112 million. Its American platform attracted more than $500 million in deposits after opening to early users in December.

The company initially required customers to withdraw money through the same payment source used to make a deposit, a common safeguard against money laundering. Management later eliminated that restriction to accelerate withdrawals, despite internal concerns that the change could increase compliance risks, the Journal reported.
Several senior U.S. executives subsequently departed, including the chief compliance officer. An outside investigation by Sullivan & Cromwell found that Polymarket
had complied with applicable regulations, according to people familiar with its conclusions.

By May, the company reportedly had reduced fraud rates to industry norms. It limited the number of debit cards that customers could connect to their accounts and hired Riskified to strengthen fraud detection.
Technology problems emerge

A second attack in July affected nearly 500 customers, according to the Journal. The alleged vulnerability allowed criminals using stolen personal information to gain access to existing accounts and their linked payment methods.
Some customers reported losing thousands of dollars and receiving little response from support staff. Polymarket
said it would reimburse affected users.

The company has since hired additional engineers, improved code reviews and expanded its risk-management team. Recent appointments include a former FBI agent and Warren Jenson, a former Amazon finance chief who became Polymarket’s
first chief financial officer.
Big valuation, bigger expectations
Coplan has spent heavily to make Polymarket
a mainstream brand. The company has signed promotional agreements with celebrities and sports organizations, including LeBron James and Major League Baseball.
At the same time, it is seeking another $1 billion from investors. Donald Trump Jr.’s 1789 Capital reportedly plans to contribute about $300 million after previously investing roughly $200 million.
The funding could help Polymarket

prepare for a possible initial public offering. It also raises the stakes for management. At a $21 billion valuation, investors are no longer backing a scrappy experiment. They are betting that Polymarket
can operate like a mature financial platform before regulators, fraudsters or dissatisfied customers force the issue.

title: Polymarket’s rapid growth raises fraud, compliance concerns
